column3: It repeats the command not to extend one's eyes toward others' allotted enjoyments, making it the closest verbal and thematic parallel to the focus.
It explicitly calls worldly possessions temporary enjoyment and adornment, then declares what is with God better and more lasting.
It identifies both hardship and good as tests, clarifying the focus's statement that worldly bloom tests its recipients.
It forbids letting one's eyes pass from devoted people in desire for worldly adornment, closely paralleling the focus's restrained gaze and worldly display.
The immediately following ayah redirects attention to prayer, patience, divine provision, and the enduring outcome of God-consciousness.
Its brief statement that people cannot be tempters in a particular respect does not clarify the worldly enjoyment that tests them.
It presents worldly gifts as temporary enjoyment and contrasts them with what is better and more lasting with God.
Musa's anger over the calf episode does not clarify the prohibition on coveting worldly display.
The earth being spread out has no useful relation to worldly adornment, testing, or lasting provision.
It states that abundance can be given in order to test people, directly clarifying the test-function of received worldly provision.
The selection of Musa and command to listen do not illuminate worldly enjoyment or its test.
Extended pillars in punishment share only a root with extending the gaze and offer no thematic support.
It describes apportioned worldly livelihood and says the Lord's mercy is better than what people accumulate, a close provision-value contrast.
It calls worldly luxury temporary enjoyment and contrasts it with the Hereafter reserved with the Lord for the God-conscious.
The extension of punishment contrasts broadly with the focus's lasting good provision, but the shared verb has a different object and setting.
The creation of pairs concerns human and animal reproduction, not the allotted classes of worldly enjoyment in the focus.
Musa's request to loosen his speech does not clarify the focus's command concerning the gaze.
The prayer not to become a test for disbelievers concerns communal vulnerability, not worldly enjoyment as a test.
It identifies wealth and children as worldly adornment and contrasts them with enduring righteous deeds that are better in reward and hope.
The remainder kept by God is called better, supporting the focus's preference for divine provision over transient gain.
Calling a people tested corrects their superstition, but it does not concern the testing role of worldly adornment.
It directly declares the Hereafter better and more lasting, compressing the focus's final value judgment.
Bearing a burden on the Day of Resurrection is in the same surah but does not clarify temporary enjoyment or provision.
The she-camel is explicitly sent as a test, giving a concrete instance of a granted thing functioning as an assay.
The production of diverse plant pairs through rain does not explain the flower-like worldly display in the focus.
The warning of punishment for denial and turning away is not a useful neighbor for the focus's material-test contrast.
Its ironic account of people falling into temptation while claiming to avoid it is a different kind of test from worldly display.
The legally mandated maintenance of widows uses enjoyment in a distinct legal sense.
Provision for people and livestock names material benefit but does not contrast it with lasting divine provision.
The threatened trial for opposing the Messenger is not the focus's test through worldly adornment.
It declares God better and more lasting, repeating the focus's decisive comparison within the same surah.
The magicians' claim about preserving an exemplary way has no meaningful relation to the focus.
It calls the angelic instruction a test and warns against disbelief, but its setting is magic rather than worldly adornment.
A stored possession in the Joseph narrative is unrelated to transient worldly display.
The command to take the staff without fear does not clarify the focus.
The testing of Musa's people by the calf is a same-surah instance of trial but not a close parallel to temporary enjoyment.
Created pairs do not illuminate the focus's classes of temporary enjoyment.
It says people delight in worldly life even though it is only temporary enjoyment compared with the Hereafter, closely supporting the focus's warning.
Harun identifies the calf as a test and redirects the people to their merciful Lord, a same-surah trial-and-redirection parallel.
It contrasts the more severe and lasting punishment of the Hereafter with worldly excess, reinforcing the focus's lasting-outcome perspective.
The Samiri's claimed perception and self-persuasion do not clarify the focus's command or its value contrast.
The extension of shadow and the sun as its indicator share imagery of extension but not the focus's restrained gaze or worldly test.
It describes people and their forebears being granted enjoyment until life grew long, a cautionary instance of extended worldly benefit.
The good destination of believers broadly complements the focus's better lasting provision but lacks its worldly-display contrast.
The extension of fruit and meat in Paradise is enduring provision, but it does not address the tested bloom of worldly life.
It names noble provision with the Lord as the reward of true believers, supporting the focus's preference for the Lord's provision.
The closing command to wait for who follows the sound path provides only a broad same-passage orientation toward the final outcome.
Extended shade in Paradise broadly contrasts with transient worldly bloom but does not directly clarify the focus.
Pairing the blessed with companions in Paradise is unrelated to the focus's warning against looking at worldly allotments.
The man's declaration of faith and command to listen do not illuminate the focus.
It names one who is tested or mad in a polemical context, not testing through worldly enjoyment.
It condemns wrongdoers for following the luxury in which they were indulged, closely illustrating the danger of worldly privilege.
The Resurrection scene's hushed voices does not clarify the focus's material or evaluative contrast.
It explicitly joins test and temporary enjoyment, though its unspecified benefit is less close than the focus's worldly bloom.
It promises believers forgiveness and noble provision, a positive counterpart to the focus's better provision from the Lord.
The measured phases of the moon do not illuminate worldly adornment, testing, or enduring provision.
It portrays someone whose response to faith reverses when tested, connecting trial to the loss of this world and the Hereafter.
It calls persecution or religious pressure a greater fitnah than killing, a distinct use of testing from the focus's worldly display.
The command to travel through the sea is unrelated to the focus's concern with coveting provision.
It explicitly identifies wealth and children as a test and contrasts them with the great reward held by God.
It calls worldly enjoyment little and the Hereafter better for the God-conscious, strongly paralleling the focus's value contrast.
God's dominion and final return offer a broad theological frame but do not clarify temporary enjoyment or the gaze.
Stretching a rope toward the sky is unrelated to extending one's eyes toward worldly allotments.
It gives believers noble provision as a lasting reward, supporting the focus's alternative to transient display.
Musa's personal trials and his mother's comfort do not clarify worldly adornment as a test.
The prayer not to be made a test for oppressors has a different object from the focus's test through enjoyed goods.
The command to take pairs into the ark does not clarify the focus's worldly enjoyment or provision contrast.
Recurring yearly tests concern heedlessness and repentance, not the tested enjoyment described in the focus.
The brothers' possessions in their account of Yusuf have no thematic relation to the focus.
It establishes that professed believers will be tested, supplying a general framework for the focus's stated test.
The final record and perfect justice do not clarify the focus's warning about worldly display.
The expectation that no trial would occur concerns Israel's blindness and deafness, not temporary enjoyment.
The pairing of corrupt and good people, with noble provision for the latter, is too remote from the focus's frame.
Sulayman's individual trial is a distinct narrative test without the focus's contrast of transient and lasting provision.
Dietary prohibitions and divine forgiveness do not illuminate the focus.
The spread of the earth and creation of fruit pairs do not clarify worldly bloom as a test.
It promises true believers forgiveness and noble provision, a positive but general counterpart to the focus's Lord-given provision.
The reinforcement by angels is not relevant to the focus's material enjoyment or test.
Yusuf's request to investigate the women concerns innocence and knowledge, not the focus.
The vision and cursed tree are a test for people, but this is a different test object and warning.
God's supply of known benefits supports the provision theme only broadly, without the focus's evaluative contrast.
It explicitly says people are made a test for one another and asks whether they will be patient, clarifying trial as a lived condition.
It contrasts desire for worldly life and its adornment with the Prophet's household's higher choice, closely echoing the focus's worldly-display concern.
It describes one group being tested through another, a social rather than material instance of the focus's test theme.
It directly addresses those who seek worldly life and its adornment, showing the insufficiency of that orientation beyond this life.
It identifies wealth and children as a test and directs attention to the great reward with God.
It forbids being impressed by wealth and children and explains that they can become means of punishment in worldly life.
It explains that testing distinguishes the truthful from the false, clarifying the assay implicit in the focus.
It repeats the warning not to be impressed by wealth and children because they can serve as punishment in worldly life.
Testing on the Fire is a punishment scene, not the present-world test through enjoyment.
The division into three groups does not clarify worldly adornment or lasting provision.
God's provision is declared inexhaustible, a close positive counterpart to the focus's provision that is better and more lasting.
The threatened taking away of the Prophet and vengeance on opponents do not illuminate the focus.
It warns against preferring family, wealth, trade, and desirable dwellings over God and His cause, closely supporting the focus's redirected attachment.
The lack of proof for associating partners does not clarify temporary enjoyment or testing.
Hypocrites' private alliance with devils does not illuminate the focus.
Calling on unresponsive beings until Resurrection is unrelated to the focus's worldly display.
No community advancing or delaying its term does not clarify the focus.
The joining of sun and moon has no useful relation to the focus's extended gaze or temporary provision.
Joyful faces on the Day of Resurrection do not clarify worldly adornment, testing, or enduring provision.
It condemns exchanging the Hereafter for worldly life, a direct value reversal of the focus's preference for what is better and lasting.
It says worldly life has been made attractive to disbelievers, supplying a close account of the display that draws the gaze.
It enumerates worldly desires made attractive to people and calls them enjoyment of worldly life before directing attention to the better return with God.
It distinguishes the reward of this world from the reward of the Hereafter, supporting the focus's evaluative contrast between temporal and lasting goods.
It calls worldly life only an enjoyment of delusion, directly sharpening the focus's warning against fixing attention on its bloom.
It contrasts those who trade worldly life for the Hereafter, providing a clear alternative allegiance to temporary gain.
It cautions against seeking the fleeting goods of worldly life and states that God possesses abundant gains.
It affirms that the reward of both this world and the Hereafter is with God, qualifying the focus's provision contrast with divine ownership of both.
It calls worldly life play and diversion and says the abode of the Hereafter is better for the God-conscious.
It warns that worldly life can deceive people, a close caution against being captured by its temporary display.
It asks who can forbid God's adornment and good provision, offering an important qualification that the focus restrains coveting rather than treating all provision as forbidden.
It describes people deceived by worldly life, directly supporting the focus's warning about its attractive bloom.
It contrasts seeking the goods of this world with God's intention for the Hereafter.
It rebukes satisfaction with worldly life in place of the Hereafter and calls worldly enjoyment little by comparison.
It describes those content with and reassured by worldly life, a negative portrait of the attachment the focus prohibits.
It compares worldly life to rain-fed vegetation that becomes flourishing and then withers, closely paralleling the focus's image of worldly bloom.
It calls worldly life a brief enjoyment before return to God, directly framing its transience.
Musa calls Pharaoh's wealth and adornment in worldly life a means by which people are led astray, a close narrative instance of dangerous display.
It describes people who prefer worldly life to the Hereafter and turn others from God's path, directly opposing the focus's value order.
It explains disbelief through preferring worldly life over the Hereafter, closely identifying the misplaced preference at stake.
It calls the enjoyment of deniers little and warns of painful punishment, reinforcing the temporary character of worldly gain.
It describes the one who seeks the immediate world and contrasts that pursuit with the intended destiny in the Hereafter.
It directs attention from differing worldly degrees to the greater degrees and preference of the Hereafter.
It calls everything made as adornment on earth a test of who is best in deed, the closest omitted parallel to the focus's worldly bloom given for testing.
It compares worldly life to vegetation raised by rain and then reduced to dry fragments, directly developing the focus's flower-like image of transient life.
It questions whether wealth and children are mistakenly taken as a hastening of good, closely interrogating the value of enjoyed abundance.
It contrasts one given a good promise to be met with one given worldly enjoyment and then brought forth for judgment.
It depicts people longing for Qarun's splendid worldly portion, a concrete instance of the covetous gaze prohibited in the focus.
It answers the desire for Qarun's splendor by declaring God's reward better for believers who are patient.
It calls worldly life diversion and play and identifies the Hereafter as the true life.
It describes people knowing only the outward aspect of worldly life while heedless of the Hereafter, a close diagnosis of attention fixed on display.
It warns that worldly life must not deceive people, directly supporting the focus's caution toward its attractiveness.
It denies that wealth and children make people nearer to God, correcting a false valuation of worldly endowment.
It warns explicitly that worldly life must not deceive people, a direct guard against the attraction described in the focus.
It calls worldly life temporary enjoyment and the Hereafter the enduring home, almost exactly restating the focus's temporal contrast.
It depicts the houses, roofs, stairs, doors, and couches that could be given as worldly display, setting up the following declaration of their transience.
Its silver ornaments and couches continue the material display that 43:35 identifies as temporary worldly enjoyment.
It identifies worldly life's deception as part of the error for which the Hereafter is denied.
It calls worldly life play and diversion and warns against being made to expend wealth, supporting the focus's devaluation of temporal goods.
It describes one who turns from remembrance and desires only worldly life, a close picture of attention diverted from the enduring good.
It calls worldly life play, diversion, adornment, rivalry, and accumulation, then compares its growth to vegetation that flourishes and withers, directly matching the focus's bloom-and-test warning.
It warns believers not to let wealth and children distract them from God's remembrance, directly complementing the focus's redirection of the gaze.
It rebukes love of the immediate life, directly opposing the focus's preference for what is better and more lasting.
It says people love the immediate life and leave behind a weighty day, closely explaining the short-sighted attachment the focus resists.
It identifies preferring worldly life as the decisive excess that leads to the Fire, directly extending the focus's value warning.
It completes the prior condition by naming preference for worldly life as the relevant choice.
It rebukes preference for worldly life immediately before declaring the Hereafter better and more lasting.
It says rivalry in accumulation distracts people, closely capturing the attention diverted by worldly displays.
